title: Battery rickshaw boom feeds lead pollution in Bangladesh
excerpt: Used e-rickshaw batteries are broken by hand and smelted near homes, bdnews24 finds. Pure Earth says 80% are recycled at informal sites.

image.alt: A worker in protective gear ladles molten recycled lead at a lead-acid battery recovery plant
image.credit: File photo: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

content:
DHAKA, 28 November 2026: The fast-growing fleet of battery-powered rickshaws and easy-bikes is feeding a cycle of lead pollution, as worn-out batteries are broken open by hand and smelted near homes and farmland, bdnews24.com reported early on Saturday (28 November) in an investigation produced with support from the Pulitzer Center.

In Charigram village in Singair, Manikganj, more than 150 residents have petitioned the authorities to stop smoke from Tanvir Enterprise, a plant that extracts lead from discarded batteries, the report said. Residents complained of eye and throat irritation, coughing and damaged crops. The factory manager, Md Habib, said the plant follows the rules. But bdnews24 found it is not on the Department of Environment's list of approved lead recycling plants, which has four facilities, although it is on the list kept by the Department of Inspection for Factories and Establishments.

In Keraniganj, reporters saw about eight workers breaking open used batteries in an open yard, some with bare hands. At a Chinese-owned battery factory in Dhamrai, Department of Environment records showed a permit to make lead-acid batteries that expired in July 2021; the documents did not show whether it was renewed.

The report cites a 2026 factsheet by the international non-profit Pure Earth, which estimates that about 4 million electric three-wheelers run in Bangladesh and that 80% of used lead-acid batteries are recycled at illegal and informal sites. Devlens checked the factsheet, which also says 15% to 20% of the lead is released into the environment each time a battery is recycled, that about 38% of children under five have elevated blood lead levels according to a national survey, and that informal recycling costs the government about Tk 915 crore ($91 million) a year in lost tax. Trade records reviewed by bdnews24 show about $112.4 million of Chinese exports of three-wheelers, battery parts and components to Bangladesh between January 2020 and June 2026.

New government rules for battery-powered rickshaws in city corporation areas, introduced on 29 October, require sellers to take back old batteries and ban dumping or burning them. The report says the rules do not answer who takes the returned batteries and how the lead is recovered.

Why it matters

Lead exposure harms children's brain development and pregnancies. The workers who break batteries and the families living near smelters are often the same low-income households that depend on the rickshaw economy. Devlens recently reported that most Dhaka battery-rickshaw drivers are migrants and unlicensed, and that Bangladesh cannot track its imports of toxic lead chromate. Health, child-protection and WASH programmes in battery-breaking areas may need blood lead testing and safer-work outreach.

What to watch

  • Whether the Department of Environment acts on the Charigram petition.
  • How the 29 October take-back rule is enforced, and whether a fee or traceability system for batteries follows, as Pure Earth has recommended.
  • Any shift from lead-acid to lithium batteries in the three-wheeler market.

Sources

  • bdnews24.com: Fast-growing battery rickshaw industry feeds a dangerous cycle of lead pollution, 28 November 2026
  • Pure Earth: The Circular Economy of Lead Acid Batteries in Bangladesh with Formal and Informal Processes (factsheet), April 2026
